```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
})

axes <- c("outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator", "sample", "weights",
          "construction", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "measure", "pred_form", "family")

curve <- read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- read_csv("data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(curve == "positive")
deviations <- read_csv("data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref <- curve |> filter(is_reference)
# every option swapped into the reproduced specification, read from the pairs file
ref_rows <- read_csv("data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(curve == "positive") |>
  semi_join(ref, by = axes)
bw <- read_csv("data/display_between_within.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
periods <- read_csv("data/display_periods.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
loo <- read_csv("data/display_loo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bailout <- read_csv("data/display_bailout.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
inference <- read_csv("data/display_inference.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
means <- read_csv("data/display_country_means.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pw <- read_csv("data/teney_panel_weights.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# fixed decimals and a true minus sign; percentages round halves up, as the
# decision map does, so that the two pages print the same figures
num <- \(x, d = 3) sub("^-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^d + 0.5) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
pe <- \(p) if (p < 0.0001) "p < 0.0001" else paste("p =", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = if (p < 0.001) 4 else 3))

# shares of a set of curve rows below zero, and below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05
below <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$r_ca < 0)
sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$r_ca < 0 & d$p_wcr < 0.05)
sig_rule <- \(col) 100 * mean(curve$r_ca < 0 & curve[[col]] < 0.05)

# one value from the fork table, the option table or the reproduced specification
fk <- \(axis, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == axis]
dv <- \(option, col, rule = NULL, which = "positive") {
  d <- deviations |> filter(curve == which, option == !!option)
  if (!is.null(rule)) d <- d |> filter(rule == !!rule)
  d[[col]][1]
}
rd <- \(option, col, rule = NULL) {
  d <- ref_rows |> filter(option == !!option)
  if (!is.null(rule)) d <- d |> filter(rule == !!rule)
  d[[col]][1]
}
bwv <- \(outcome, predictor, col) bw[[col]][bw$outcome == outcome & bw$predictor == predictor]
perv <- \(sample, col) {
  periods |>
    filter(sample == !!sample, outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "unemp", copredictor == "none",
           estimator == "fe_twoway", pred_form == "raw") |>
    pull(all_of(col))
}
per_sig <- \(sample) {
  d <- periods |> filter(sample == !!sample, predictor == "unemp")
  100 * mean(d$r_ca < 0 & d$p_wcr < 0.05)
}
loo_two <- loo |> filter(estimator == "fe_twoway", left_out != "none")
loo_cty <- loo |> filter(estimator == "fe_country", left_out != "none")
vs <- \(cc) loo$variation_share[loo$estimator == "fe_twoway" & loo$left_out == cc]
bav <- \(group, col) {
  bailout |>
    filter(group == !!group, outcome == "mcosmo", predictor == "unemp", estimator == "fe_twoway") |>
    pull(all_of(col))
}
inf <- \(est, rule, col) inference[[col]][inference$estimator == est & inference$inference == rule]

level_share <- \(ax) sum(forks$share[forks$axis %in% ax])
# the questions fixed by the four Level 1 decisions that vary on the curve, and
# whether the measurement decisions and the form split each one across classes
questions <- curve |>
  mutate(cls = r_ca < 0 & p_wcr < 0.05) |>
  summarise(straddle = any(cls) & !all(cls), .by = c(outcome, predictor, copredictor, estimator))
twoway <- curve |> filter(estimator == "fe_twoway")
country <- curve |> filter(estimator == "fe_country")
```

This page sets out every decision that an analysis of the claim has to make, the options that each decision offers, and whether each option is a justifiable way of answering the claim. The claim, in the wording that SCORE took from the paper of the original author (OA) [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], is that "poor national economic performances significantly decrease positive EU-framing dimensions". The course reads it as a claim about change within countries over time, that is, about whether the citizens of a member state framed the EU less in positive terms than before as the economy of their country deteriorated, in the member states of 2004–2013. The [case page](index.qmd#sec-questions) sets out the hypothesis from which the claim was taken and the data on which it rests.

Fourteen decisions stand between those data and a verdict on the claim, and most of them offer more than one option that a competent analyst might choose. The course has asked of every option one question, whether it is a justifiable way of answering this claim, and the options that are have been crossed into the 864 specifications of the curve of the claim. The curve is therefore the set of justifiable answers that the course recognises, and the disagreement that remains on it is disagreement between defensible analyses. The options that left the curve are taught on this page in full, because each of them either answers a different question or answers this one less well, and working out which of the two applies, and why, is a large part of understanding what the claim asks. The [decision map](map.qmd) draws the same menu as a path from the data to a verdict, with every option selectable and its effect on the estimand statement and on the results shown as it is selected.

The decisions are of three kinds, and the menu is arranged by them. Some change **what is being estimated**, so that two people who choose differently are answering different questions and their results are not rival estimates of one quantity. Some change **how a named quantity is measured** and leave the question as it is. And some change neither, only how the model is fitted and how uncertain its answer is said to be. On the curve, the Level 1 decisions that vary carry `r pct(level_share(c("outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator")))` of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation as main effects, the four measurement decisions together `r pct(level_share(c("noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "measure")))` and the form of the predictor `r pct(level_share("pred_form"), 2)`, with `r pct(fk("interactions"))` in the interactions between decisions. Most of what moves the results on the curve is therefore a choice between questions, which is why the reasons for a choice have to be given at the level to which the choice belongs.

## The estimand statement

Write the statement that your analysis will complete:

> Among **which country-years**, with **each counting how much**, the association between **poor economic performance**, measured as **X**, and **positive EU framing**, measured as **Y**, comparing **what with what**, **holding what fixed**.

Move one decision and reread the statement. If a bold slot other than the two "measured as" slots changes, you have made an estimand decision. If only a "measured as" slot changes, you have made a measurement decision. If nothing in the statement changes, you have made an estimation decision, because the statement names what is estimated and says nothing about how the model is fitted or tested. The completed statement is your estimand [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand], and it is what a reader has to know before your coefficient means anything.

The test sorts decisions relative to the statement that you wrote, and a statement written differently would sort them differently. Written finely enough to name the published series behind the unemployment rate, every decision on the menu would rewrite it, and written as loosely as "the economy and EU framing", none would. The statement is written at the resolution of the claim, which names the constructs and the comparison and not the figures that stand for them. One decision lies on the boundary between Level 1 and Level 2, whether the answers of a respondent enter as a share of their own mentions or as a count of the items in the set. Both are built from the same thirteen items, which is a reason to call the choice a matter of measurement. But a share and a count remain different quantities however well the items were measured, one the weight of a framing among the frames that a person holds and the other its volume, and because two people who differ on the rule would not accept each other's number as an estimate of the same thing, the menu places the scoring rule at Level 1.

Two decisions at Level 2 change the statement more than their level suggests, and both are easy to miss. Scoring respondents who mention nothing as zero keeps every respondent in the cell mean, but the mean then equals the share among those who answered multiplied by the proportion who answered, so that the outcome mixes how people frame the EU with whether they name any meaning of it at all. And a published series that covers only part of the panel is chosen as a measure of the predictor, yet it changes the population of the question as well, since the country-years that the series does not cover drop out of the analysis, and the decision map marks both changes in the statement at the moment that they are made.

## The curve of 864 {#the-curve}

The curve crosses, for each of the three positive scales scored as shares, the options that answer the claim: unemployment in four published series and in two forms, or GDP growth in the World Bank series; with or without the other economic measure held fixed; two-way or country fixed effects; respondents who mention nothing scored zero or left out; all 13 items or the 12 without "unemployment"; and cells as interviewed or weighted. That gives 256 unemployment and 32 growth specifications for each scale, 288 per scale and 864 in all. Four decisions take a single option on the curve: all 270 country-years, no regression weight, the share as the scoring rule, and a linear model.

Every point is placed by its descriptive partial correlation, aligned with the claim so that below zero is the direction that the claim predicts, and classed by a restricted wild cluster bootstrap by country, which allows for the correlation of the residuals of a country from year to year and for the few countries that carry most of the variation. Of the `r nrow(curve)` specifications, `r pct(below(curve))` lie below zero and `r pct(sig(curve))` lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05; the partial correlations run from `r num(min(curve$r_ca))` to `r num(max(curve$r_ca))`, with a median of `r num(median(curve$r_ca))`. The reproduced specification, the cosmopolitan share on World Bank unemployment under two-way fixed effects with respondents who mention nothing scored zero, gives b = `r num(ref$b, 5)`, t = `r num(ref$t)` on `r ref$df` df and r = `r num(ref$r)`, the value that the reproduction task targets, and its bootstrap p-value is `r num(ref$p_wcr)`.

Almost every specification on the curve points in the direction of the claim, so the uncertainty that remains concerns the strength of the evidence rather than its direction, and it is divided mainly by two decisions. Under country fixed effects `r pct(sig(country))` of the specifications lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, against `r pct(sig(twoway))` under two-way fixed effects; with unemployment as the predictor the shares are `r pct(sig(filter(country, predictor == "unemp")))` and `r pct(sig(filter(twoway, predictor == "unemp")))`, while with growth they are `r pct(sig(filter(curve, predictor == "growth")))` under both designs. @tbl-forks gives, for every decision that varies on the curve, the share of the variance that it carries and how often moving it alone changes the class of a specification.

| Decision | Level | Share of the variance | Class changes when moved alone |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Estimator | 1 | `r pct(fk("estimator"))` | `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Predictor | 1 | `r pct(fk("predictor"))` | `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Frame set | 1 | `r pct(fk("outcome"))` | `r pct(fk("outcome", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Adjustment set | 1 | `r pct(fk("copredictor"))` | `r pct(fk("copredictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Item set | 2 | `r pct(fk("item_set"))` | `r pct(fk("item_set", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Respondents who mention nothing | 2 | `r pct(fk("noop"))` | `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Published series | 2 | `r pct(fk("measure"))` | `r pct(fk("measure", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Cell weighting | 2 | `r pct(fk("cell_weight"))` | `r pct(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Predictor form | 3 | `r pct(fk("pred_form"))` | `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` |
| Interactions | – | `r pct(fk("interactions"))` | – |

: The decisions that vary on the curve of 864. The share of the variance is the share of the variance of the claim-aligned partial r that the decision carries as a main effect; the class changes are the share of pairs of specifications, differing only in that decision, whose members fall in different classes (below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, or not). The predictor pairs raw World Bank unemployment with World Bank growth. Source: `data/spec_curve_forks.csv`. {#tbl-forks}

The numbers on this page come from files that the course pipeline writes: the curve is `data/spec_curve.csv`, the comparison of every option on the menu with its twins on the curve is `data/menu_deviations.csv`, one row per pair in `data/menu_deviations_rows.csv.gz`, and the displays of the findings that left the curve are the `data/display_*.csv` files. `data/menu_options.csv` holds the label, the status and a one-sentence reason for every option discussed below, and the helpers of the browser lab and of the workspace read it to explain an option that is off the curve.

## Level 1 – Estimands {#level-estimand}

Each decision at this level rewrites the estimand statement, so that two analysts who make it differently are answering different questions.

| Decision | On the curve | Off the curve, and where it is taught | Share of the variance | Class changes |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| **Frame set** | cosmopolitan `mcosmo` · utilitarian `mutil` · positive composite `mpos` | communitarian `mcomm` · libertarian `mlib` · negative composite `mneg`, on a curve of their own | `r pct(fk("outcome"))` | `r pct(fk("outcome", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Scoring rule** | share of mentions `share` | count of items `count` · count per item `rate`, on [The items behind the scales](../../companion/measurement.qmd) | fixed | – |
| **Predictor** | unemployment `unemp` · GDP growth `growth` | – | `r pct(fk("predictor"))` | `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Adjustment set** | none `none` · the other measure `other` | – | `r pct(fk("copredictor"))` | `r pct(fk("copredictor", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Sample** | all 270 country-years `all` | 2004–2008 `y2004_2008` · 2009–2013 `y2009_2013` · without the bailout countries `no_bailout` · without Greece and Spain `no_GR_ES`, on [The multiverse and its critics](../../companion/multiverse.qmd) | fixed | – |
| **Whose average** | each country-year once `none` | respondents `n_cell` · effective sample size `n_eff` · adult population `pop`, on [Weights](../../companion/weighting.qmd) | fixed | – |
| **Estimator** | two-way fixed effects `fe_twoway` · country fixed effects `fe_country` | random effects `re` · pooled OLS `pooled_cl` · within–between model `rewb`, on [the statistical methods page](../../companion/stats-methods.qmd) | `r pct(fk("estimator"))` | `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` |

: The seven estimand decisions. The last two columns describe the curve, as in @tbl-forks; "fixed" marks a decision with a single option on the curve. {#tbl-level1}

### Frame set

OA groups the thirteen answer options of the question on what the EU means to the respondent into four dimensions, which cross the valence of a meaning with its content: cosmopolitan (positive and non-materialist), utilitarian (positive and materialist), communitarian (negative and non-materialist) and libertarian (negative and materialist), with a positive and a negative composite built from the two pairs. The claim names the positive dimensions, so the cosmopolitan scale, the utilitarian scale and the positive composite are its outcomes. The composite is the plainest reading of "positive EU-framing dimensions", the cosmopolitan scale is the one that the instruction for the second Multi100 task asked the analysts to use, and the utilitarian scale is the materialist dimension, on which the first hypothesis expects the stronger effect. On the curve the three give `r pct(sig(filter(curve, outcome == "mcosmo")))`, `r pct(sig(filter(curve, outcome == "mutil")))` and `r pct(sig(filter(curve, outcome == "mpos")))` of specifications below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, and the frame set carries `r pct(fk("outcome"))` of the variance on the curve.

The three negative scales answer the other half of the first hypothesis, an increase in negative framing, and they have a curve of their own, `data/spec_curve_negative.csv`, aligned so that below zero is the direction of that half. They are not independent evidence for the claim. Under the share rule the four scales of a respondent sum to one, and when respondents who mention nothing are scored zero, the positive and the negative composites of every country-year add up to one minus the share of respondents who mention nothing; within countries the aligned negative composite and the positive composite correlate at 0.93, so a 'confirmation' on the negative composite largely counts the positive result a second time. The communitarian scale also contains the item "unemployment", which ties the outcome to the predictor by content: removing the item cuts its aligned correlation at the reproduced specification from −0.495 to −0.290. The libertarian scale, finally, shows almost no association, and on the negative curve only `r pct(dv("mlib", "below_zero_sig", which = "negative"))` of its specifications lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, against `r pct(dv("mcomm", "below_zero_sig", which = "negative"))` for the communitarian scale and `r pct(dv("mneg", "below_zero_sig", which = "negative"))` for the negative composite. How the thirteen items hang together is examined on [The items behind the scales](../../companion/measurement.qmd).

### Scoring rule

The scoring rule decides what "more" of a framing means. The share, the measure of the paper, divides the items of a scale that a respondent mentions by all the items that the respondent mentions, so it is a relative frequency: whatever else a respondent mentions lowers the share of every scale. The count is the number of the items of the scale that a respondent mentions, whatever else they mention, and the rate divides the count by the number of items in the scale, so that a two-item and a five-item scale stand on one footing. The claim concerns how citizens frame the EU, which is a matter of composition, and the share is the only rule on the curve.

The count measures something else, the volume of what people say about the EU. Across the country-years the cosmopolitan count correlates `r num(cor(pw$c_mcosmo, pw$mean_items), 2)` with the mean number of items that respondents mention, against `r num(cor(pw$w_mcosmo, pw$mean_items), 2)` for the share, and the two constructions of the cosmopolitan outcome correlate only `r num(cor(pw$w_mcosmo, pw$c_mcosmo), 2)`. A count therefore answers a neighbouring question, whether people say more or fewer positive things about the EU, and it is the construct that KEVF1 and 018OL used, which matters for reading their results. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the count leaves `r pct(dv("count", "below_zero_sig"))` of them below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, against `r pct(sig(curve))` on the curve, and at the reproduced specification it moves the aligned correlation from `r num(ref$r_ca)` to `r num(rd("count", "r_ca_dev"))` (bootstrap `r pe(rd("count", "p_dev"))`). The rate gives exactly the same test and partial correlation as the count in a linear model, since it divides the count by a constant; it is the form of the count that a beta regression can take.

### Predictor

The claim names "poor national economic performances", and the paper models two measures of it, the national unemployment rate and annual GDP growth, both of which are justifiable readings and both of which stay on the curve. Unemployment is also the measure that the instruction for the second Multi100 task named. Growth carries less information within countries, because 59% of its variation within countries is common to all of them in the same year, above all the recession of 2009, which the year effects of the two-way design remove. Its slope within countries on the cosmopolitan scale is small (`r num(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "b_within"), 5)`, bootstrap `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "p_within_wcr"))`), while across the 27 country means the association is clear (`r num(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "b_between"), 4)`, `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "growth", "p_between"))`). The claim expects framing to rise with growth, so the sign of every growth specification is reversed on the curve. Moving from unemployment to growth, with everything else fixed, changes the class of `r pct(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, and growth specifications lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 in `r pct(sig(filter(curve, predictor == "growth")))` of cases, against `r pct(sig(filter(curve, predictor == "unemp")))` for unemployment.

### Adjustment set

With unemployment as the predictor, leaving growth out gives the association of framing with unemployment whatever happened to output, and holding growth fixed gives the association at a given rate of growth; with growth as the predictor the roles swap. Neither measure is a confounder of the other in the usual sense, since both are expressions of the same crisis, so the two options are two estimands rather than a right and a wrong set of controls, and both stay on the curve. The unadjusted slope is the one that the reproduced specification estimates, and the adjusted one follows the model of the original study, which carries both measures. Under the principle that the controls which define an estimand belong in every model of it [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational], the two are better kept as two estimands, each with its own definition, than mixed as interchangeable variants of one. Whether growth is a common cause, a second expression of the downturn or a step on the path from the crisis to framing is a question for the [causal graph](../../companion/dags.qmd). On the curve the decision carries `r pct(fk("copredictor"))` of the variance and changes the class of `r pct(fk("copredictor", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs.

### Sample

The population of the claim is the 27 member states over 2004–2013, the 270 country-years of the panel, and it is the only sample on the curve. Each of the four restrictions on the menu answers a question about a different population, which is why the sample sits at Level 1, and none of them is a second way of answering the claim as written. The restrictions are conventionally run as robustness checks, but a check that changes the population changes the estimand statement, and its result cannot confirm or undermine an answer about another population.

- **2004–2008** keeps only the years before the crisis reached most labour markets. A window that contains no crisis cannot speak to whether the crisis undermined positive framing; within countries it measures how framing tracked the smaller fluctuations of those years.
- **2009–2013** keeps only the crisis years, so it drops the comparison with the period before them and asks how framing moved with the deepening and easing of the crisis once it had begun.
- **Without the bailout countries** removes the eight countries that received financial assistance (Cyprus, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Portugal, Romania and Spain), in which the crisis was deepest and which carry most of the variation in unemployment that identifies the slope. The question becomes whether the association holds in the countries in which the crisis was mild.
- **Without Greece and Spain** is an influence diagnostic, a check on how much the result owes to the two countries with the largest rises in unemployment, of the kind that @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed lists among the forms of nonequivalence as unstable country subsets. A single hand-picked exclusion is a weak form of the diagnostic, which leaving out one country at a time does more completely.

Splitting the panel at 2008 is one rung of a ladder of ways to handle the crisis years: pool them with the other years, as the full panel does; shift them with an indicator for the crisis years; split the panel into periods; or absorb every year with its own effect, as the two-way design does. The course considered the middle rung, a crisis indicator, and left it out of the menu, because OA measures the crisis continuously, through growth, unemployment and fiscal transfers, so that a period indicator would partial out the very variation that the claim is about, and because the year effects of the two-way design absorb such an indicator exactly.

Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the four restrictions leave `r pct(dv("y2004_2008", "below_zero_sig"))` (2004–2008), `r pct(dv("y2009_2013", "below_zero_sig"))` (2009–2013), `r pct(dv("no_bailout", "below_zero_sig"))` (without the bailout countries) and `r pct(dv("no_GR_ES", "below_zero_sig"))` (without Greece and Spain) below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, against `r pct(sig(curve))` on the curve, and the sign changes in `r pct(dv("no_bailout", "sign_changes"))` of the pairs without the bailout countries. Three displays keep these findings in the course without mixing populations on the curve. For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(perv("all", "b"), 5)` on the full panel (bootstrap `r pe(perv("all", "p_wcr"))`), `r num(perv("y2004_2008", "b"), 5)` on 2004–2008 (`r pe(perv("y2004_2008", "p_wcr"))`) and `r num(perv("y2009_2013", "b"), 5)` on 2009–2013 (`r pe(perv("y2009_2013", "p_wcr"))`), so each period on its own gives a steeper slope than the panel as a whole. In the two-way design Greece holds `r pct(vs("GR"))` of the variation in unemployment that is left after the fixed effects, Spain `r pct(vs("ES"))`, Poland `r pct(vs("PL"))` and Ireland `r pct(vs("IE"))`; leaving out one country at a time moves the slope between `r num(min(loo_two$b), 5)` and `r num(max(loo_two$b), 5)`, and `r sum(loo_two$p_wcr < 0.05)` of the 27 refits reach bootstrap p < 0.05, while in the country design `r sum(loo_cty$p_wcr < 0.05)` of 27 do. And the slope is `r num(bav("bailout", "b"), 5)` in the eight bailout countries (Webb `r pe(bav("bailout", "p_wcr_webb"))`, since eight clusters allow only coarse Rademacher p-values) and `r num(bav("other", "b"), 5)` in the other nineteen (`r pe(bav("other", "p_wcr"))`), a difference with bootstrap `r pe(bav("difference", "p_wcr"))`. Read together, the displays suggest that the association is concentrated in the countries where the crisis was deepest, which is what a reader of the claim needs to know, and which the curve alone, with its single population, cannot say.

### Whose average

Unweighted, every country-year counts once and the slope describes the average member state, which matches a claim about how national economies shape the framing of their citizens. Malta then counts as much as Germany. Weighting by the number of respondents in a country-year (`n_cell`) or by their effective number, discounted for the unevenness of the survey weights (`n_eff`), is a precision argument: if the cell means differed only in how precisely they are measured, weighting by sample size would estimate the same quantity more efficiently. Weighting by adult population (`pop`) changes the quantity to the average European, in which the largest member state counts `r num(max(pw$pop_15plus) / min(pw$pop_15plus), 0)` times as much as the smallest.

Only the unweighted fit stays on the curve. The precision argument fails on these data, because sampling error is a small part of the variation that the weights are meant to correct: across the 270 cells the sampling variance of a cell mean of the cosmopolitan share averages 0.000103, against a residual variance of 0.00141 in the reproduced model, so about 7% of the unexplained variation is sampling noise and the rest is genuine variation between country-years. Under those conditions efficient weights are close to equal, and weights that run from `r format(min(pw$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(pw$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` respondents (a ratio of `r num(max(pw$n_cy) / min(pw$n_cy), 1)`) buy little precision and mostly shift weight towards the years with two survey waves and towards the countries with the largest samples. The design effects are small (median `r num(median(pw$deff), 2)`, maximum `r num(max(pw$deff), 2)`), so the effective sample size behaves almost exactly like the respondent count. The population weight answers a defensible but different question, which the claim does not ask, and [Weights](../../companion/weighting.qmd) sets it out as an alternative estimand. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, the respondent weight leaves `r pct(dv("n_cell", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, the effective sample size `r pct(dv("n_eff", "below_zero_sig"))` and the population weight `r pct(dv("pop", "below_zero_sig"))`, which changes the class of `r pct(dv("pop", "class_changes"))` of the pairs.

### Estimator

The estimator decides which country-years are compared with which, and it is the decision that moves results most on the curve, with `r pct(fk("estimator"))` of the variance. Two fixed-effects designs stay on it, as two estimands. Two-way fixed effects removes the stable differences between countries and whatever all member states went through together in a year, so the slope compares each country with itself, relative to the common European path. Country fixed effects keeps the changes that were common to Europe in a given year, which on this panel make up 29% of the variation in unemployment within countries, so its comparison includes the common path; its slope is larger, and it is open to confounding by any shift in framing across Europe that coincided with the crisis. At the reproduced specification the two give r = `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "r_descriptive"))` (bootstrap `r pe(inf("fe_twoway", "wcr_rademacher", "p"))`) and r = `r num(inf("fe_country", "conventional", "r_descriptive"))` (bootstrap `r pe(inf("fe_country", "wcr_rademacher", "p"))`), and across the curve moving between them changes the class of `r pct(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs. Year effects are the last rung of the ladder that is described under the sample.

**Pooled OLS** regresses framing on unemployment across all 270 country-years at once, so its slope mixes the stable differences between countries with the changes within them. On these data the two run in opposite directions. Of the variance of unemployment, 46.5% lies between countries, as does 65.1% of the variance of the cosmopolitan share, and the slope across the 27 country means is positive (`r num(bwv("mcosmo", "unemp", "b_between"), 5)`, `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "unemp", "p_between"))` on 25 df), while the slope within countries is negative (`r num(bwv("mcosmo", "unemp", "b_within"), 5)`). A pooled slope therefore answers neither the within-country reading of the claim nor the cross-national one, which a regression on the country means answers more cleanly, and models without fixed effects are the first of the kinds of nonequivalent model that @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed names. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, pooled OLS leaves `r pct(dv("pooled_cl", "below_zero"))` of them below zero and `r pct(dv("pooled_cl", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, and the sign changes in `r pct(dv("pooled_cl", "sign_changes"))` of the pairs, which is how a different quantity behaves rather than a noisy version of the same one.

**Random effects** fits one slope that is a weighted blend of the within-country and the between-country associations, and it is consistent only if the stable differences between countries are unrelated to the predictor. That assumption fails here: on the course panel the within and the between slopes have opposite signs in `r sum(sign(bw$b_within) != sign(bw$b_between))` of the `r nrow(bw)` combinations of positive scale and predictor, and the test of their difference rejects at the 5% level in `r sum(bw$p_difference < 0.05)` of them. Because each country is observed ten times, the blend lies close to the within slope (in the audit of the menu, a median of 4% of the way towards the between slope), so the estimator weakens the within-country slope a little and imports a little of the opposite association between countries; and since it has no year effects, it resembles the country design more than the two-way one. Swapped into the specifications of the curve, it leaves `r pct(dv("re", "below_zero_sig", "re_cr1_g1"))` below zero with p < 0.05 under errors clustered by country, a figure that owes as much to the comparison it makes as to the evidence.

**The within–between model** of @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects separates what random effects blend: the deviation of the predictor from its country mean carries the within slope, the country mean carries the between slope, and a random intercept for country keeps the multilevel structure. Its within slope equals the fixed-effects slope exactly, so as a point on the curve it would repeat existing points with other errors, and its place is in the teaching, where it shows the two associations side by side; for the cosmopolitan scale the test of their difference gives `r pe(bwv("mcosmo", "unemp", "p_difference"))`. The model is set out on [the statistical methods page](../../companion/stats-methods.qmd).

## Level 2 – Measurement {#level-measurement}

The question stays fixed, and these decisions change how a named construct becomes a column of numbers.

| Decision | On the curve | Off the curve, and where it is taught | Share of the variance | Class changes |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| **Respondents who mention nothing** | scored zero `zero` · left out `drop` | split rule `split` · multiple imputation `mi_mice`, `mi_amelia`, on [Missing answers](../../companion/missingness.qmd) | `r pct(fk("noop"))` | `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Item set** | all 13 items `all` · without "unemployment" `un` | – | `r pct(fk("item_set"))` | `r pct(fk("item_set", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Cell weighting** | as interviewed `unweighted` · weighted `design` | – | `r pct(fk("cell_weight"))` | `r pct(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Published series** | unemployment: World Bank `wb_nat` · Eurostat 15–74 `es_1574_act` · Eurostat 20–64 as a share of the population `es_2064_pop` · Labour Force Survey 25–64 `es_2564_lfs`; growth: World Bank `wb_growth` | Eurostat table tipsun20 `es_1574_tips` · Eurostat growth `es_growth`, on [Social science data sources](../../companion/data-sources.qmd) | `r pct(fk("measure"))` | `r pct(fk("measure", "crossing_rate"))` |

: The four measurement decisions, with the last two columns as in @tbl-forks. {#tbl-level2}

### Respondents who mention nothing

Of all respondents, `r pct(100 * sum(pw$n_noop) / sum(pw$n_cy))` mention none of the 13 items, and under the share rule they have no share at all, so something has to be decided about them. Scoring them zero is the rule of the course panel and of the reproduced specification, and it keeps every respondent; but it changes the construct, since the cell mean then equals the share among those who answered multiplied by the proportion who answered, so that the rate of saying nothing enters every scale. Leaving them out is consistent with the share as a measure, since a respondent with no mentions has no share, and it is what the code of the original study did; its cost is that it conditions on answering. Within countries the rate of saying nothing falls slightly as unemployment rises (b = −0.0011 per point; t = −1.25 with errors clustered by country), so the zero rule pulls the slopes a little towards zero. Both rules stay on the curve, where the drop rule gives `r pct(sig(filter(curve, noop == "drop")))` of specifications below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 and the zero rule `r pct(sig(filter(curve, noop == "zero")))`.

The split rule leaves out those who said "don't know" or gave no answer and scores off-list answers as zero, a compromise whose construct is no clearer than that of either rule on the curve, and its results lie close to theirs (`r pct(dv("split", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05). The two imputation rules fill in the shares of the silent respondents from age, sex, education and the country-year under a missing-at-random assumption. They are principled, but they were computed only at the standard measurement settings (raw unemployment in the World Bank series, all items, cells as interviewed), so they cannot be crossed with the rest of the menu, and their `r dv("mi_mice", "n_pairs")` specifications are tested by a clustered test pooled over the imputations rather than by the bootstrap. [Missing answers](../../companion/missingness.qmd) sets out what each rule assumes about the people who stayed silent.

### Item set

OA builds every scale from the 13 items of the paper, and the code of the original study also builds a second version without the item "unemployment", which leaves the communitarian scale and every denominator one item shorter. When more people name "unemployment" as a meaning of the EU, every other share falls mechanically, so part of a decline in positive shares can be the rise of that one item rather than a change in how positively the EU is framed. Both sets stay on the curve, and the shift between them is the part of the result that the overlap carries: with all items `r pct(sig(filter(curve, item_set == "all")))` of specifications lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, and without "unemployment" `r pct(sig(filter(curve, item_set == "un")))`. Under the reduced set a respondent whose only mention was "unemployment" has nothing left and joins the respondents who mention nothing.

### Cell weighting

The cell mean can be the mean of the respondents as interviewed, as in the original study and the course panel, or the mean under the post-stratification weight supplied by GESIS, which estimates the mean of the national population. The weighted mean is the better estimator of a national quantity in principle, but the design effects are small, and the decision carries `r pct(fk("cell_weight"), 2)` of the variance on the curve and changes the class of `r pct(fk("cell_weight", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs. Both options stay on the curve; if a leaner menu were wanted, this would be the first decision to fix.

### Published series

The five analysts merged five different unemployment series, which differ in age band and denominator. The four that cover all 270 country-years move together within countries, correlating between 0.995 and 0.999 once country and year means are removed, and all four stay on the curve, where the decision carries `r pct(fk("measure"))` of the variance. The Eurostat table tipsun20, which KEVF1 merged, is a different matter: it has no row for the United Kingdom and, before 2009, rows only for France and Sweden, so choosing it leaves `r rd("es_1574_tips", "n_cells_dev")` of the 270 country-years. That is a decision about the sample presented as a decision about the measure, and its results describe another population and another period; swapped into the unemployment specifications of the curve, it leaves `r pct(dv("es_1574_tips", "below_zero_sig"))` of them below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, a figure that probably reflects the crisis years, which make up most of its cells, more than the series itself. The Eurostat growth series has no row for the United Kingdom either, so it removes a country from the population, and only the World Bank growth series stays on the curve.

## Level 3 – Estimation {#level-estimation}

With the question and the measures fixed, these decisions change the model that is fitted and how sure its answer is said to be. Two of the three concern the fit and can move the estimate; the third concerns the inference and moves only the class.

| Decision | On the curve | Off the curve, and where it is taught | Share of the variance | Class changes |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| **Predictor form** | raw `raw` · logged `log` (unemployment only) | – | `r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)` | `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` |
| **Outcome family** | linear `gaussian` | beta regression `beta`, on [the statistical methods page](../../companion/stats-methods.qmd) | fixed | – |
| **Inference** | wild cluster bootstrap by country `wcr` | CR2 with Satterthwaite df `cr2` · clustered, CR1 `cr1` · conventional `conventional` · bootstrap with Webb signs `wcr_webb`, on [the statistical methods page](../../companion/stats-methods.qmd) | nil | – |

: The three estimation decisions: two about the fit, one about the inference. The inference cannot change the partial correlation, so its share of the variance is nil. {#tbl-level3}

### Predictor form

Unemployment enters raw, so that each percentage point counts the same, or logged, so that each proportional rise counts the same and a rise from 4% to 8% counts as much as one from 10% to 20%. Both are defensible statements of how a crisis might act on framing, and the claim does not choose between them, so both stay on the curve. Growth takes negative values and enters raw only. Centring and standardising are not separate analyses, because shifting or rescaling the predictor cannot move t, r or p. The form carries almost none of the variance on the curve (`r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)`), yet moving it alone changes the class of `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs.

### Outcome family

The linear model fits the cell means directly; the beta family fits them through a logit link with a likelihood that respects the bounds of a share. Both describe the same conditional mean, and neither is a different answer to the claim. The bounds matter for the utilitarian scale, whose cell means come close to zero, while the cosmopolitan and positive cell means lie well inside the unit interval. The beta family barely moves the results: swapped into the specifications of the curve it leaves `r pct(dv("beta", "below_zero_sig"))` below zero with p < 0.05 under errors clustered by country, and its median shift in the aligned correlation is `r num(dv("beta", "median_shift"))`. It stays off the curve because the bootstrap that classes the curve is written for linear models, so keeping it would put two inference rules on one curve, and it serves instead as a check of the functional form, available for the share and the rate but not for the count, which is not a proportion.

### Inference

All the inference rules estimate the same slope and differ only in how uncertain they say it is. Conventional errors treat the 270 country-years as independent, which they are not: in the reproduced model the residuals of a country correlate 0.53 from one year to the next. Errors clustered by country allow any correlation within a country, at the price of resting on 27 clusters, and the variation that identifies the slope is concentrated in a few of them, so that the 27 clusters behave like about ten. The standard clustered errors (CR1, tested on 26 df) assume clusters of similar influence and overstate the evidence when that is not so. The CR2 correction with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and the restricted wild cluster bootstrap are two remedies for few or unbalanced clusters, and the curve is classed by the bootstrap, with CR2 stored beside it as a check; on the curve the Satterthwaite df of CR2 have a median of `r num(median(curve$df_cr2), 1)`, which says how many countries effectively carry the information.

@tbl-inference gives the reproduced specification under each rule. The partial correlation stays the same throughout, but the p-value runs from below 0.001 to above 0.1, which is why the course does not call the reproduced result significant at 5% without saying under which errors. Across the curve, the share of specifications below zero with p < 0.05 is `r pct(sig_rule("p_conv"))` under conventional errors, `r pct(sig_rule("p_cr1"))` under CR1, `r pct(sig_rule("p_cr2"))` under CR2, `r pct(sig_rule("p_wcr"))` under the bootstrap and `r pct(sig_rule("p_wcr_webb"))` under the bootstrap with Webb signs.

| Rule | t | df | p | r from the conversion formula |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Conventional | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "t"))` | `r inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "df")` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "p"), 5)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "r_formula"))` |
| Clustered by country, CR1 | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "t"))` | `r inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "df")` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "p"))` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr1_g1", "r_formula"))` |
| CR2, Satterthwaite df | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "t"))` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 1)` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "p"))` | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "cr2_satterthwaite", "r_formula"))` |
| Wild cluster bootstrap, Rademacher | – | – | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "wcr_rademacher", "p"))` | – |
| Wild cluster bootstrap, Webb | – | – | `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "wcr_webb", "p"))` | – |

: One estimate under five kinds of inference: the reproduced specification, b = `r num(ref$b, 5)`, whose descriptive partial correlation is `r num(ref$r)` under every rule. Source: `data/display_inference.csv`. {#tbl-inference}

The last column explains why the curve plots the descriptive partial correlation and tests it separately. The conversion r = t / sqrt(t^2^ + df) recovers the partial correlation only from the conventional t and the residual df; fed a clustered t and its smaller df, it returns a larger number although the evidence is weaker. The conventional option stays in the course as the instructive mistake, since the move of the reproduced specification from p = `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "conventional", "p"), 4)` to p = `r num(inf("fe_twoway", "wcr_rademacher", "p"))` shows that a decision which leaves the estimate untouched can decide whether a result is reported as significant.

## Admissible combinations {#admissibility}

Not every combination of options exists, and the browser lab and the workspace tell you when you have combined two that do not go together:

- **Published series ← predictor.** The unemployment series go with unemployment and the growth series with growth.
- **Predictor form ← predictor.** GDP growth takes negative values and enters raw only.
- **Imputed answers ← the standard settings.** The two imputation engines were run with raw unemployment in the World Bank series, all items and cells as interviewed, so they combine only with those settings.
- **Outcome family ← scoring rule.** The beta family needs a proportion strictly between 0 and 1: the share and the rate qualify, the count does not.
- **Off-curve options ← one at a time.** Each option off the curve was fitted against the specifications of the curve with every other decision on its curve options, so a combination of two off-curve options, such as a count under pooled OLS, was never fitted.

---

## Claim alignment {#the-claim-alignment-step}

Every outcome on the curve is a positive framing, for which the claim predicts a **negative** coefficient on unemployment, so for unemployment specifications the partial correlation needs no alignment: below zero is the direction of the claim. One flip remains. When the predictor is GDP growth, the claim predicts a **positive** coefficient on the positive framings, so the claim-aligned value multiplies b, t and r by −1 (the lab applies this for you), and after the flip below zero means the direction of the claim for every specification on the curve, whatever it measures.

The negative scales have their own curve, on which the alignment is reversed so that below zero is the direction of the other half of the first hypothesis, an increase in negative framing. Reversing the sign of r there is equivalent to reverse-coding the negative scale as 1 − y before fitting, which flips the sign of the coefficient and leaves its standard error, |t| and p-value untouched. Alignment changes the direction in which the evidence is stated and nothing about the evidence itself.

---

## Worked example

**Choice:** frame set `mpos`, scoring rule `share`, predictor `unemp`, adjustment `none`, sample `all`, whose average `none`, estimator `fe_twoway`; respondents who mention nothing `drop`, item set `all`, cell weighting `unweighted`, series `wb_nat`; form `raw`, family `gaussian`, inference by the wild cluster bootstrap by country.

**Justification, by level.** The claim speaks of positive dimensions in the plural, which the composite scale captures more directly than the cosmopolitan scale alone, and the share is kept because the claim concerns how people frame the EU rather than how much they say about it. The comparison that the claim makes is that of a country with itself as its economy deteriorates, net of whatever all member states went through together in a year, which is what two-way fixed effects estimate; nothing in the claim restricts the countries or the years, and the claim is about countries, so every country-year counts once. Respondents who mention nothing are left out, following the code of the original study, because a person with no framing of the EU is not a person with zero positive framing, and the World Bank series is kept because it is the series on which the panel was built. The raw percentage is kept because the claim gives no warrant for a proportional effect, and the slope is tested by the wild cluster bootstrap by country, because the residuals of a country correlate from year to year and a few countries carry most of the variation.

A justification of this kind makes a specification defensible, because it connects each choice to the wording of the claim or to an argument about the data, at the level to which the choice belongs.

---

## Preregistration {#preregistering-your-choice}

Fix your specification in a preregistration **before you run it**. That is what stops you picking the path that happens to give the answer you want. You preregister it by completing the preregistration block in your report *before* you add the model-fitting code, and you run the model only after that. It is a real template, the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" shortened to five fields, so the exercise mirrors what a registered secondary-data analysis actually does.

- **In the workspace:** the report skeleton (`index.qmd`) contains the preregistration block in Task 5. Fill in your choices and their justification, and **run `prereg()` before you write the model code below it**. The printed declaration, which the rendered report keeps above the cells that fit the specification, is your preregistration.
- **On the browser lab page:** there is no render step, so complete the commented preregistration block and copy it into your notes. That copy is your preregistration.

An optional mirror form may be used to log preregistrations from the class, and the link is shared in the session. It is not required. The completed block in your report is your official preregistration.

---

## Reporting a result {#reporting-your-result}

After running your model, submit your result to the class-results form. You do not fill it in by hand and you do not transcribe anything: `report_result()` reads your preregistered choices, builds the specification label with your choices in it, and prints a link to the form with your result already filled in, on the claim-aligned scale. Open it and press Send, and your result appears on the live [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) chart.

Each submission carries the t and the df of the conventional fit and the descriptive partial correlation that the helper computes from them, $r = t / \sqrt{t^2 + df}$, the conversion that Multi100 used and the one that the curve uses for its vertical axis, and the chart places the submission by that correlation. The class of a submission, significant at 5% or not, is read by looking its specification up in the curve, so that every point on the class chart is classed by the same bootstrap as the curve.

In the workspace the helper is defined in `R/spec_tools.R`, which the report and the working script both source; on the [Browser lab](lab.qmd) page it is already loaded:

```r
source("R/spec_tools.R")
report_result()
```

This prints your submission link, ready to click.

## Justifying each decision {#what-each-decision-commits-you-to}

### The statement first

Before defending any single choice, complete the estimand statement. The first slot is which country-years, and your sample decides it, together with any published series that covers only part of the panel. The second is how much each country-year counts, and your weighting decides it. The two "measured as" slots are your predictor and outcome constructs, and every Level 2 decision concerns how one of them is measured, although the rule for respondents who mention nothing reaches into what the outcome means. The outcome construct is itself two decisions, which meanings count and what "more" of them means, and both rewrite the statement. The last slots are what your estimator compares and what your adjustment holds fixed. A Level 1 decision changes a bold slot other than the two "measured as" slots, and that is what separates it from the decisions on the other two levels.

### Reasons at each level

A Level 1 decision needs an argument from the claim, since it chooses the question: which framing the claim is about, which measure of the economy, which comparison and which population. A Level 2 decision needs an argument from the instrument and the data, such as the content overlap between an outcome item and the predictor, or what a respondent who says nothing has told the survey. A Level 3 decision needs an argument from the structure of the data, such as the bounds of a share or the correlation of a country with itself over time. An option off the curve can still be the right choice for a different question, and a reason of the right kind will usually say which question that is.

### One specification and the whole curve

A decision can carry almost none of the variance on the curve and still decide whether *your* result clears p = 0.05, because significance is a property of one specification and variance is a property of the whole set. The rule for respondents who mention nothing carries `r pct(fk("noop"))` of the variance and changes the class of `r pct(fk("noop", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs; the predictor form carries `r pct(fk("pred_form"), 2)` and changes `r pct(fk("pred_form", "crossing_rate"))`. Pin the question on the four Level 1 decisions that vary on the curve, leave the measurement decisions and the form free, and `r sum(questions$straddle)` of the `r nrow(questions)` questions still contain both a specification below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 and one that is not, which is why you fix your specification in the preregistration before you run it.
